title: Κύων καὶ λαγωός
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 182. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Κύων θηρευτικὸς λαγωὸν συλλαβών, τοῦτον ποτὲ μὲν ἔδακνε, ποτὲ δὲ αὐτοῦ τὰ χείλη περιέλειχεν.
sentences.tr: Kyōn thēreutikos lagōon syllabōn, touton pote men edakne, pote de autou ta cheilē perieleichen.
sentences.l: A hunting dog, having caught a hare, at one moment would bite him, and at another would lick the hare's lips all round.
sentences.i: A hunting dog caught a hare, and now would bite him, now lick him about the lips.
sentences.n: ποτὲ μέν … ποτὲ δέ is 'at one moment … at another', and the two imperfects make both actions repeated rather than done once. αὐτοῦ is a possessive genitive — the lips are the hare's, not the dog's — standing outside the article it belongs with (αὐτοῦ τὰ χείλη). περιλείχω is to lick all round — the affectionate motion, which is why the hare cannot tell what is happening to him.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀπαυδήσας ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, παῦσαί με καταδάκνων ἢ καταφιλῶν, ἵνα γνῶ πότερον ἐχθρὸς ἢ φίλος μου καθέστηκας. »
sentences.tr: Ho de apaudēsas ephē pros auton· « All’, ō houtos, pausai me katadaknōn ē kataphilōn, hina gnō poteron echthros ē philos mou kathestēkas. »
sentences.l: And he, having grown weary of it, said to him: « Come now, you there, stop biting me or kissing me, so that I may know whether you have come to be my enemy or my friend. »
sentences.i: The hare, at the end of his endurance, said to him: « Come, you — stop either biting me or kissing me, so that I may know whether you have turned out my enemy or my friend. »
sentences.n: ἀπαυδάω is to give out, to be worn past bearing. παῦσαι is the aorist middle imperative with a supplementary participle for what is to stop, and the participles agree with the dog who is doing it — με is the object of the biting and the kissing, not of the stopping. ὦ οὗτος is the blunt Greek hail, 'you there'. καθέστηκας, perfect of καθίστημι, is 'you have come to stand as, have turned out to be'.

sentences.t: Πρὸς ἄνδρα ἀμφίβολον ὁ λόγος εὔκαιρος.
sentences.tr: Pros andra amphibolon ho logos eukairos.
sentences.l: Against an ambiguous man the story is well-timed.
sentences.i: The story is well aimed at the man who can be taken two ways.
sentences.n: ἀμφίβολος is what can be taken two ways at once — the man whose bearing gives no sign which side he is on. The εὔκαιρος formula again, with no copula written; ἐστί is left to be understood, as regularly in these morals.
